newsitem.title: UK: Chase "significantly underweight" in U.S. equities.
newsitem.headline: Chase "significantly underweight" in U.S. equities.

text.p: Chase Manhattan Bank's global asset management operations are significantly underweight in U.S. equities, which are seen as expensive, with Japan and the UK offering little value.
Mark Richardson, Chase's chief investment officer, global asset management, told Reuters in an interview it was difficult to find value in the major markets currently.
"If you believe the three biggest markets are all relatively unattractive it becomes quite tough to be overweight equities," he said.
He said Chase's global equity allocations were running underweight U.S. and Canada, UK and Japan and overweight in continental Europe, Latin America and South-East Asia.
Chase, with over $120 billion funds under management, had taken some money out of equities in its U.S. funds and was running overweight on bonds.
He said about two to three percentage points had been cut from equity allocations in U.S. funds in January when the market was rising.
Globally, Chase had recently cut equities to a 51 percent allocation from 53 and raised cash to nine percent.
"We are a little bit wary to say the least...It is very hard to see that you are going to make a huge amount of money, even in bond markets, from here," Richardson said.
"We can see pockets of value but it is hard to be a raging bull at the moment."
In the U.S. he said an economic slowdown was expected, and inflation could tend higher, pressuring markets.

"If you think in terms of what is driving markets, it is strong growth and benign inflation. I think you are going to continue to get reasonable growth and continuing reasonable inflation but I think the trends are going to both be in the wrong direction."
He said quarterly annualised inflation of 3.5 percent was possible in the U.S. for two quarters, which could be negative for the market, and raise the prospect of a Fed tightening.
He said he expected bond yields in the U.S. to rise and then come down again later in the year.
He saw "a lot of room for disappointment" in U.S. equities.

"We are significantly underweighting the U.S. at 34 percent versus 45 (in the MSCI index weighting). Value for us is a problem and from here we don't believe we are going to get much support from the bond market.

"I am always nervous at any market which is depending on its forward momentum, really on cash flow. Cash flow obviously sustains markets for a time but somewhere along the line if the fundamentals don't justify it then you are riding for a fall. I don't know if we have got there yet."
"Our prediction is that the first quarter will be all right but I'd be minding my eye from then onwards.
There was value in small cap stocks as managers had been buying index stocks recently, and in most cyclicals excluding retail.
He said it was crucial to other markets that any U.S. market correction was limited.
He said Chase was overweight in continental Europe.
Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will give consumers power and make conditions a lot more competitive for companies.
"The name of the game in Europe is going to be bottom up with less attention to country allocations. I think there are going to be big winners and big losers."
"There is an enormous amount of pressure to restructure and downsize. The knack is to be able to identify the companies doing the right thing and focusing shareholder value."

He said Japanese equity market strength could continue until the financial year end at the end of March, but there was uncertainty after that banks needing to take equity market gains to offset loan write-offs.
He said Chase has been underweight in Japan, although a possible sell-off in the second quarter could provide a buying opportunity.
Latin America should make up for what many analysts felt was a disappointing 1996, he said. -- London newsreel +171 542 6880.
